'''''Faidherbia''''' is a genus of [[Fabaceae|fabaceous]] plants containing one species, '''''Faidherbia albida''''', which was formerly widely included in the genus ''[[Acacia]]'' as ''Acacia albida''. The species is native to [[Africa]] and the [[Middle East]] and has also been introduced to [[Pakistan]] and [[India]].<ref name="ILDIS">[http://www.ildis.org/LegumeWeb?sciname=Faidherbia+albida ILDIS LegumeWeb]</ref> Common names include '''apple-ring acacia'''<ref>C.Michael Hogan, ed. 2010. [http://www.eol.org/pages/648064 ''Faidherbia albida''. Encyclopedia of Life.]</ref> (their circular, indehiscent seed pods resemble apple rings),<ref name=wpa1>{{cite web |last1=Armstrong |first1=W. P. |title=Unforgettable Acacias, A Large Genus Of Trees & Shrubs |url=http://waynesword.palomar.edu/plaug99.htm |website=Wayne's Word |access-date=17 November 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151110064020/http://waynesword.palomar.edu/plaug99.htm |archive-date=10 November 2015 }}</ref> '''white acacia''',<ref name="Shmida2005">{{cite book |last=Shmida |first=Avi |title=MAPA's Dictionary of Plants and Flowers in Israel |publisher=MAPA Publishers |location=Tel-Aviv|year=2005 |page=260|language=he|oclc=716569354}}</ref> and '''winter thorn'''.<ref name="ILDIS"/> The [[South Africa]]n name is '''ana tree'''.<ref name="ILDIS"/><ref name=vanWyk>{{cite book |last1=van Wyk |first1=Braam |last2=van Wyk |first2=Piet |date=1997 |title=Field Guide to trees of southern Africa |location=Cape Town |publisher=Struik |page=500 |isbn=1-86825-922-6}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
This species has been known as ''Acacia albida'' for a long time, and is often still known as such. Guinet (1969) in [[Puducherry (city)|Pondicherry]] first proposed separating it into the genus ''Faidherbia'', a genus erected during the previous century by [[Auguste Chevalier]] with this as the [[type species]], seconded by the South African James Henderson Ross (1973) and the [[Senegal]]ese [[legume]] botanist Nongonierma (1976, 1978),<ref name=Sahel>{{cite journal |last=Geerling |first=Chris |date=15 July 1982 |title=Guide de terrain des ligneux Saheliens et Soudano Guineens |journal=Mededelingen Landbouwhogeschool Wageningen |volume=82 |issue=3 |pages=177, 178 |language=fr}}</ref> but authors continued to favour classification under ''Acacia'' as of 1997.<ref name=vanWyk/><ref name=Sahel/>

===Infraspecific variability===
According to [[John Patrick Micklethwait Brenan]], as written in the ''[[Flora of Tropical East Africa ]]'' (1959), two forms can be distinguished in this region ([[Kenya]], Tanzania, [[Uganda]]).  Race A is distinguished by generally smooth features, whereas race B is more hairy. Ross (1979) notes that all trees in the south of central Tanzania belong to race B.<ref name="fao">FAO: [http://www.fao.org/docrep/006/Q2190E/Q2190E10.htm Handbook on Seeds of Dry-Zone Acacias]</ref> Similarly, Nongonierma described two variants for Senegal, var. ''glabra'' and var. ''pseudoglabra'', but his distinction was disregarded taxonomically as of 2007.<ref name=apd/>

==Description==
Faidherbia is a thorny [[tree]] growing up to  {{convert|6–30|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall and up to {{convert|2|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} in trunk diameter. Its deep-penetrating [[tap root]] makes it highly resistant to drought. The bark is grey, and fissured when old.

==Distribution==
In [[Southern Africa]], it is absent from most of the territory, avoiding dry, colder and upland areas or areas of [[Climate of South Africa|winter rainfall]], but it does occur in the eastern [[Caprivi Strip]], the northern [[Okavango Basin|Okavango]] basin, the floodplains of the [[Linyanti River|Linyanti]], [[Zambezi]] and [[Limpopo River|Limpopo]] rivers, as well as southwards to [[Gaborone]]. In [[Zimbabwe]], the tree is absent from the [[Eastern Highlands|highlands]] and central plateau, but it does occur in [[Gonarezhou National Park|Gonarezhou]]<ref name="cun1">{{cite web |last1=Cunliffe |first1=Rob |last2=Muller |first2=Tom |last3=Mapaura |first3=Anthony |title=Vegetation survey of Gonarezhou National Park, Zimbabwe (Final report) |url=https://gonarezhou.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/GNP-Vegetation-Report.pdf |website=gonarezhou.org |publisher=Frankfurt Zoological Society et al. |access-date=6 April 2023 |date=August 2012}}</ref> and southwards to the [[Kruger National Park|Kruger Park]] and adjacent [[lowveld]] of western [[Gaza Province|Gaza]] and southern [[Maputo Province|Maputo]] provinces. It reaches its southern limit along the [[Pongola River|Pongola]] floodplain in [[Maputaland]].<ref name=vanWyk/> In western [[Namibia]], it is present in the [[Kaokoveld]], [[Damaraland]], and the [[Namib-Naukluft National Park|Namib-Naukluft]] area.

In the rest of Africa, it is absent from deserts, areas of high rainfall, [[tropical rainforest]]s and mountainous areas, but occurs throughout the eastern half of the continent from the southern coast in [[Maputaland]] to [[Egypt]], throughout the [[Subsahara]]n [[Sahel]] and the [[Horn of Africa]]. In Northern Africa, besides in Egypt it also occurs in [[Algeria]], it does not occur in [[Morocco]] proper, but is found in [[Western Sahara]].<ref name="ILDIS"/>

In Asia, it is thought to be native to [[Yemen]] and [[Saudi Arabia]] in the [[Arabian Peninsula]], [[Iran]], and in the [[Levant]] in Israel, [[Syria]] and [[Lebanon]].<ref name="ILDIS"/> In Israel, the tree is protected by law.<ref name="Shmida2005"/>

A population is found in [[Relict (biology)|relict]] groves in [[Israel]] (in the [[Shimron]] nature reserve, near the [[community settlement (Israel)|community settlement]] of [[Timrat]], and in the western-most reaches of the [[Valley of Elah]]). All of the trees in a given grove are genetically identical and seem to have multiplied by [[vegetative reproduction]] only, for thousands of years.{{Citation needed|date=October 2011}}

Introduced populations are found in [[Cyprus]], [[Pakistan]], and India ([[Karnataka]]), as well as on [[Ascension Island]].<ref name="ILDIS"/>

==Ecology==
In Southern Africa, it usually grows on alluvial floodplains in bushveld, on riverbanks or flood pans, in swamps, or in dry watercourses that can flood during rains.<ref name=vanWyk/> It grows in woodland in the Sahel, along the Zambezi, and in [[Sudan]].<ref name="ILDIS"/> In the Sahel, it grows gregariously in groves. It also grows in savannahs in Sudan and the Sahel, in heavy soils with good drainage.<ref name=Sahel/>

In tropical eastern Africa, it sometimes occurs singly, but may often be the dominant species in dry woodlands.<ref name=apd/> In the Sahel, it has an irregular, clumped distribution, absent in some areas, but occurring in others.<ref name=Sahel/>

It grows in areas with {{convert|250–600|mm|in|abbr=on|frac=2}} of rain per year.<ref name="fao"/>

==Uses==
''Faidherbia albida'' is important in the Sahel for raising [[bee]]s, since its flowers provide bee [[Forage (honeybee)|forage]] at the close of the rainy season, when most other local plants do not.<ref name="world">[https://web.archive.org/web/20070928031700/http://www.worldagroforestry.org/Sites/TreeDBS/aft/speciesPrinterFriendly.asp?Id=1 World AgroForestry]</ref>
[[File:Foliage of White Acacia (Faidherbia albida).jpg|thumb|Foliage of Faidherbia albida in early summer]]
The seed pods are used for raising [[livestock]], are used as [[camel]] [[fodder]] in [[Nigeria]],<ref name="world"/> and are eaten by stock and game in Southern Africa.<ref name=vanWyk/> They are relished by elephant, antelope, buffalo, baboons and various browsers and grazers, though strangely ignored by warthogs and zebras.<ref>{{cite journal | journal = Journal of Tropical Ecology | volume = 6  | issue = 4 | date = 1990 | pages = 445–457 | title = Fruit production by ''Acacia albida'' trees in Zambezi riverine woodlands | author = Kevin M. Dunham | doi = 10.1017/S0266467400004843| s2cid = 85090695 }}</ref>

The wood is used for [[canoes]], [[mortars and pestles]], while the bark is pounded in [[Nigeria]] and used as a packing material on pack animals. The wood has a density of about 560 kg/m<sup>3</sup> at a water content of 12%.<ref name="fao2">FAO: [http://www.fao.org/docrep/V5360E/v5360e0f.htm Role of acacia species in the rural economy of dry Africa and the Near East]</ref> The energy value of the wood as fuel is 19.741 kJ/kg.<ref name="world"/>

Ashes of the wood are used in making soap and as a [[depilatory]] and tanning agent for hides. The wood is used for carving and the thorny branches useful for a natural barbed fence.<ref>VITA (1977) {{full citation needed|date=March 2016}}</ref> Pods and foliage are highly regarded as livestock fodder. Some 90% of Senegalese farmers interviewed by Felker (1981) collected, stored, and rationed ''Acacia albida'' pods to livestock.{{citation needed|date=May 2023}} Zimbabweans use the pods to sedate fish. Humans eat the boiled seeds in times of food scarcity in Zimbabwe.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}}

It is valued in [[agroforestry]] as it [[nitrogen fixation|fixes nitrogen]], and a high yield has been achieved in at least one test plot of maize crops grown amongst the trees at a density of 100 to 25 tree per hectare.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bayala|first1=Jules|last2=Larwanou|first2=Mahamane|last3=Kalinganire|first3=Antoine|last4=Mowo|first4=Jeremias G.|last5=Weldesemayat|first5=Sileshi G.|last6=Ajayi|first6=Oluyede C.|last7=Akinnifesi|first7=Festus K.|last8=Garrity|first8=Dennis Philip|date=2010-09-01|title=Evergreen Agriculture: a robust approach to sustainable food security in Africa|url=http://www.evergreenagriculture.net/sites/default/files/Evergreen%20Agriculture%20Garrity%20et%20al%20Food%20Security.pdf|journal=Food Security|language=en|volume=2|issue=3|pages=197–214|doi=10.1007/s12571-010-0070-7|s2cid=12815631|issn=1876-4525|access-date=2016-03-02|archive-date=2012-10-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121021144226/http://evergreenagriculture.net/sites/default/files/Evergreen%20Agriculture%20Garrity%20et%20al%20Food%20Security.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> According to a 2018 article in ''[[The Guardian]]''{{which|date=July 2025}}{{fact|date=July 2025}}, [[monoculture]]s of this species are popular in parts of [[Niger]], where it is known as ''gao'' in [[Hausa language|Hausa]], to use for [[intercropping]].{{full citation needed|date=July 2025}}[[File:White Acacia foliage.jpg|thumb|Green foliage of White Acacia (Faidherbia albida)]]

<ref name="Don'tTrustGuardian">{{Cite news | url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2018/aug/16/regreening-niger-how-magical-gaos-transformed-land | title=The great African regreening: Millions of 'magical' new trees bring renewal| newspaper=The Guardian| date=2018-08-16| last1=MacLean| first1=Ruth}}</ref> It is also used for [[erosion control]].{{citation needed|date=September 2019}} Its value as an agroforestry tree lies partially in the fact that the tree drops its leaves during the rainy season, and therefore does not compete with crops for sunlight.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Becking |first1=David |title=Faidherbia albida |url=http://treesa.org/faidherbia-albida/ |website=Trees SA |access-date=24 December 2020}}</ref> The trees' use in farmer-managed natural regeneration of degraded soils throughout southern Niger since the 1990s has been described by one writer as "the biggest positive environmental transformation in the Sahel, and possibly in Africa".<ref>{{cite book |editor-last=Villalón |editor-first=Leonardo |date=2021 |title=''The Oxford Handbook of the African Sahel''|publisher=Oxford University Press |pages=209–230 |chapter=Chapter 11: Land Use Change and Climate-Smart Agriculture in the Sahel |isbn=9780198816959}}</ref>

=== Medicinal uses ===
An extract is used to treat ocular infections in [[farm]] animals.<ref name="world" /> The bark is used in traditional medicine in Southern Africa,<ref name="vanWyk" /> and Niger.<ref name="Don'tTrustGuardian" />

==Cultural significance==
[[File:Dense grove of White Acacia (Israel).jpg|thumb|Stand of White acacia trees growing in a thicket]]
''Faidherbia albida'' is known in the [[Bambara language]] as ''balanzan'', and is the official tree of the city of [[Segou]] on the [[Niger River]] in central [[Mali]].<ref>[https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/africa/1960425.stm BBC News story on Mali's ''Faidherbia albida'' trees]</ref> According to legend, Segou is home to 4,444 ''balanzan'' trees, plus one mysterious "missing tree" – the location of which cannot be identified.{{citation needed|date=September 2019}}

In [[Serer language|Serer]] and some of the [[Cangin languages]], it is called ''Saas''. [[Serer creation myth#Saas|Saas]] figures prominently in the [[Serer creation myth|creation myth of the Serer people]]. According to the myth, it is the [[tree of life]] and fertility.<ref name="Serer civilisation">{{in lang|fr}} [[Henry Gravrand|Gravrand, Henry]], "La civilisation [[Serer people|sereer]]", vol. II : Pangool, Nouvelles éditions africaines, [[Dakar]], 1990, pp. 125–127, {{ISBN|2-7236-1055-1}}</ref>
